title: Van Meegeren: the forger who fooled the Nazis
summary: The 'Vermeers' that fooled a nation, the sale to Göring, the confession — and the chemistry that still identifies his work.

shots.title:
The Vermeer
that wasn't.
shots.subtitle: Han van Meegeren (1889–1947)
shots.narration: In 1937 the Netherlands celebrated the discovery of a new Vermeer. It had been painted that very year, by a frustrated painter named Han van Meegeren.

shots.text: Hailed as Vermeer's **masterpiece** — compared to the Night Watch.
shots.narration: Dutch art historians hailed 'The Supper at Emmaus' as Vermeer's masterpiece and compared it in importance to Rembrandt's Night Watch.

shots.label: paid by **Museum Boijmans** for 'The Supper at Emmaus'
shots.context: It beat the Rijksmuseum to the purchase.
shots.narration: Museum Boijmans in Rotterdam beat the Rijksmuseum to it, paying 520,000 guilders.
The Rijksmuseum later paid 1.3 million guilders for another of his 'Vermeers'. One curator privately called it bad and crude — but his doubts stayed in his diary.

shots.text: After the war: a 'Vermeer' in **Göring's** collection.
shots.narration: After the war, a 'Vermeer' was found in the collection of Hermann Göring. Van Meegeren had sold it — and was arrested for collaborating with the Nazis, a capital charge.
His defence was astonishing: the painting was not Dutch heritage at all, because he had painted it himself. To prove it, he painted another 'Vermeer'.

shots.text: Convicted of **forgery and fraud** — dead before serving his year.
shots.narration: The charge became forgery and fraud. He was sentenced to one year in prison, and died in 1947 before serving it.

shots.heading: How he beat the tests
items: It passed the alcohol-swab and hot-needle tests
shots.narration: An early plastic, Bakelite, hardened his paint so it passed the age tests of the day, and he scraped old paintings to reuse their canvases. Even so, nineteenth-century pigments slipped in.

shots.text: **Lead-210**: a radioactive clock inside lead white.
shots.narration: In 1967 scientists showed how to tell old lead white from new, using lead-210: once lead is refined from ore, its excess lead-210 decays with a 22-year half-life.
Today Bakelite is his fingerprint. A copy of Baburen's 'Procuress' at the Courtauld showed no modern pigments, but traces of Bakelite confirmed it as Van Meegeren's work in 2011.

A chemist had already caught him
questions.explain: Selling Dutch heritage to the Nazis carried a possible death sentence; forgery did not.

questions.prompt: What did Bakelite do for his forgeries?
options: Hardened the paint so it passed the alcohol-swab and hot-needle tests
questions.explain: Hard paint resisted both period tests — but Bakelite is easy to detect with modern instruments.

questions.prompt: Why did he reuse old canvases?
options: An old canvas looks — and dates — old, hiding the new paint
questions.explain: Reusing a period support is a classic tactic; it is why examiners date the paint as well as the support.

questions.prompt: What is the half-life of lead-210, in years?
questions.explain: Freshly refined lead carries excess lead-210 that decays with a 22-year half-life — a clock for lead white.
